narrative:
The model determined that you have an 82% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this predicted risk is so high, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your class rank at the end of your third year was the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Your first-year class rank was the second most important factor and also pulled the outcome toward not passing. These two academic-standing measures outweighed everything else. Your undergraduate GPA was the third most influential piece of information, but it worked in the opposite direction, giving a modest pull toward eventual success.

In practical terms, your first- and third-year class ranks placed you in the second decile, far below the average ranks of roughly sixth and fifth decile among students who were accepted. Your LSAT score of 31 and undergraduate GPA of 2.9 were also noticeably lower than the averages of accepted applicants (37 and 3.23 respectively). Your upper-middle family income and plan to attend full-time were typical and did not meaningfully affect the result.

The school’s decision was based solely on these academic performance signals, not on your gender or race. To improve your chances, you should focus on raising your class standing if you retake courses, consider retaking the LSAT to boost that score, or explore schools with different admissions thresholds that weigh other strengths. Strengthening these core academic indicators will be the most direct way to shift future predictions in your favor. (248 words)
